implementation_notes: Swift's `lazy var real: Image = Image.load(path)` is the pattern in the language: the initial value is not calculated until the first time the property is used, and it is stored afterwards. The documentation is explicit that a lazy property must be a var, and that simultaneous first access from several threads gives no guarantee that it is initialized only once - unlike stored type properties, which are guaranteed to be initialized exactly once even under concurrency. So a shared stand-in needs an explicit lock, an actor, or a static, while a property wrapper is the reuse route when the deferral logic (plus locking) must be applied to several properties.
pitfalls: lazy var is not thread-safe: simultaneous first access can run the initializer more than once, so a shared stand-in must add a lock, an actor or a static rather than relying on the keyword.
A lazy property must be a var and cannot be read through a let-bound reference to a struct, because the first access mutates the instance.
A lazy initializer closure that captures self keeps the stand-in (and everything it holds) alive, which is a classic retain-cycle source when combined with a delegate or observer.
